title: Ignitability and stiffness map in (T, p, phi)
summary: A three-dimensional scatter of temperature, pressure and equivalence ratio, coloured by a stiffness ratio and marked where the mixture does not ignite, with the training region outlined. It shows where a surrogate model is being asked to extrapolate.

media.alt: Three-dimensional scatter of temperature, log pressure and equivalence ratio coloured by stiffness ratio with red crosses for non-igniting cases and an orange box for the training region.
media.caption: Reference render with synthetic demonstration data (design-system gallery).

source.note: Plot class from the design system's plot taxonomy; synthetic demonstration data.

read_the_figure.question: Where is the chemistry stiff or non-igniting?
read_the_figure.axes: x: temperature in K (800 to 1800). y: log10 of pressure in atm. z: equivalence ratio phi. Colour: log10 of the stiffness ratio (about 3.1 to 4.8). Crosses: non-igniting cases.
look_at: Where do the crosses (non-igniting) cluster? Here: cold and low-pressure corner.
Where is the stiffness largest (bright yellow)? It grows with temperature.
How much of the cloud lies outside the orange training box?
Is the view angle hiding a corner? Rotate in an interactive version.
read_the_figure.proves: It shows the domain where a model was trained and where the underlying chemistry is hard to integrate or does not ignite, so the user knows where predictions are interpolation and where they are extrapolation. It does not show model error.
if_wrong: No outline of the training region: the reader cannot tell interpolation from extrapolation.
Colour scale without units or without the definition of stiffness: the number has no meaning.
Static 3D view only: depth ambiguity hides points behind others.

terms.meaning: Ratio of the fastest to the slowest relevant decay rates of the linearised system, from the eigenvalues of the Jacobian.
Whether the mixture auto-ignites within the simulated time. Non-igniting cases are marked separately.
The box of (T, p, phi) values used to fit a surrogate or neural model; outside it predictions are extrapolation.
A two-dimensional cut through the cloud at a fixed value of the third variable; the alternative to a 3D view.

remember: Stiffness S = max|Re lambda| / min|Re lambda| of the Jacobian; plot log10 S.
Orange box = where you trained. Everything outside is extrapolation.
Crosses are cases that do not ignite: do not average them in.
3D scatter needs a stated view, an interactive version or 2D slices.

understand.title: Marks and encodings
understand.text: Three position channels give the thermodynamic state (T, log p, phi); colour (viridis, light to dark) encodes log stiffness for igniting points; red crosses encode a categorical outcome, no ignition; orange edges draw the training box. Marker size is constant, so size carries no data.

understand.title: Why this form answers the question
understand.text: The question has four dimensions and a category: state, stiffness and outcome. A 3D scatter keeps all of it in one picture and gives a feel for the shape of the domain; the box is the one object that turns a descriptive cloud into a statement about model validity. Stiffness appears on a log scale, because it spans orders of magnitude.

understand.title: Read this reference render
understand.text: Q1: Where do the non-igniting cases sit? On the left, around T below about 950 K and at low p (log10 p below about 0.9): the red crosses cluster there. Q2: Where is the stiffness highest? Toward the front-right of the box at high T, the yellow dots at about 4.6 to 4.8 (stiffness ratio near 5e4). Q3: Is the training box covering the igniting region? It covers T from 1000 to 1500 K, p from 1 to 20 atm, and phi 0.5 to 1.5; a visible share of the yellow, hottest points near T = 1700 K lies outside, so a model trained there would be extrapolating exactly where it is stiffest.

understand.title: The must-check list, explained
understand.text: Training region outlined: the orange box is the content of the claim. Without it the plot only describes the data. With it you can count what fraction of the physically relevant domain the model has seen and what lies beyond.

understand.title: How it misleads
understand.text: 3D perspective makes depth hard to read: a point may look inside the box and be outside. Colour and size are not accurate for numbers. Random points imply coverage that is not systematic: empty regions are not proof of non-ignition. Log p instead of p changes how distances look. Overlapping points hide each other.

understand.title: Alternatives
understand.text: Three or four 2D slices (T against p at several phi) with the box as a rectangle, which read much more accurately. A heat map of ignition delay over (T, p) at phi = 1. A table of the training bounds.

understand.title: A variant to create
understand.text: Redraw as a 2 by 2 panel of slices, each with the training rectangle and the crosses, sharing one colour bar.

steps.title: Stiffness ratio from eigenvalues
steps.note: The Jacobian of the species equations has widely separated eigenvalues.

steps.title: Explicit stability limit and the cost
steps.note: Forward Euler is stable only for h below 2 over the fastest rate, no matter how smooth the solution is.

worked.title: What stiffness 1e4 costs an explicit solver
worked.problem: Fastest decay rate |lambda_max| = 1e6 1/s, slowest 1e2 1/s, final time 1 ms. Find S, log10 S, and the number of explicit Euler steps.

solution.text: Largest stable step and steps to reach 1 ms.

worked.answer: log10 S = 4, which sits in the middle of the colour bar; an explicit method needs at least 500 steps, a stiff implicit method far fewer.
